In upholding section 43, the majority of the Court provided considerable guidance to the interpretation of the provision. The majority held that the person administering the discipline must be a parent or legal guardian, or in some cases, a school teacher (i.e. non-parental relatives such as grandparents, aunts, or uncles, as well as babysitters and other caretakers, are banned from spanking); that the force must be used "by way of correction" (sober, reasoned uses of force that address the actual behaviour of the child and are designed to restrain, control or express some symbolic disapproval of his or her behaviour), that the child must be capable of benefiting from the correction (i.e. not under the age of 2 or over 12), and that the use of force must be "reasonable under the circumstances", meaning that it results neither in harm nor in the prospect of bodily harm. Punishment involving slaps or blows to the head is harmful, the Court held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-33) Use of any implement other than a bare hand is illegal and hitting a child in anger or in retaliation for something a child did is not considered reasonable and is against the law. The Court defined "reasonable" as force that would have a "transitory and trifling" impact on the child. For example, spanking or slapping a child so hard that it leaves a mark that lasts for several hours would not be considered "transitory and trifling".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-34)
Among the recommendations of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, formed to redress the legacy of the Canadian Indian residential school system, is a call to repeal Section 43 of the Criminal Code.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-35)
On 23 March 2021, the Senate of Colombia unanimously voted to approve a bill that prohibits physical punishment, cruel, humiliating, or degrading acts, and violence as forms of correctional approaches for the upbringing of children and adolescents in Colombia.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-36)

Until 2026, the Czech Republic had remained the only country in the European Union that does not outlaw child corporal punishment or plan to introduce such a law.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-37) On July 17, 2025, the president signed an amendment to the Civil Code, making corporal punishment of children explicitly prohibited by law, beginning January 1, 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-cz-16)
Corporal punishment in schools in Denmark became explicitly prohibited in 1967 and in 1985, parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children became outlawed through a new law which required parents "to protect their child from physical and psychological violence and other humiliating treatment".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-39) However, the law was believed to still support corporal punishment as there was a controversy whether the law permitted parents to punish their children physically or otherwise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-40) Therefore, after several years of debate, a new, clearer law came into force on 28 May 1997, providing that "_The child has right to care and security. It must be treated with respect for its person and must not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment_".
Denmark's autonomous territories, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, banned corporal punishment of children in 2007 and 2016, respectively.

School corporal punishment was banned in 1914.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-41) Parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was outlawed in 1969 when the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, stating that a "petty assault" was not punishable if committed by parents or others who exercise their right to chastise a child, was removed. In 1983, corporal punishment of children was explicitly banned.
In the Napoleonic era parents were explicitly allowed to physically punish their children. Spanking was previously popular, with 85% of French parents admitting to using it. However, in 2019, the National Assembly approved a bill introducing a complete ban on all forms of physical punishment of children and required mayors officiating at civil weddings to remind couples that violence against children is unlawful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-auto-7) The law makes corporal punishment a civil offense, not a criminal one.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-42)
School corporal punishment was prohibited in East Germany (which became part of the Federal Republic of Germany at the German reunification on 3 October 1990). In the Federal Republic (West Germany before reunification), it was prohibited at different times in its different states between 1975 and 1983.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-43)

In the Federal Republic of Germany, in 1980 it became prohibited for parents to educate their children with "degrading measures" (it was not clear exactly what "degrading" meant), of which the common interpretation was that corporal punishment of children was still permitted as long as it was not "degrading". On 1 July 1998, corporal punishment was outlawed through a new law stating that "Degrading educational measures, especially physical and psychological maltreatment, are inadmissible"; the common interpretation of that law was that parents still had some right to use corporal punishment on their children. In November 2000, that law was replaced with a new more clear and strict law stating that "_Children have right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological violence and other degrading educational measures are inadmissible._"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-45)
The 2006 enacted Law 3500/06 on the treatment of domestic violence prohibits the use of physical violence against a minor as a means of punishment in the context of his upbringing, with the explicit clarification - in the explanatory memorandum - that corporal punishment is not included. to the permissible penitentiary measures of article 1518 of the Civil Code and that its use entails for the parents the consequences of the bad exercise of parental care.
Specifically, Article 4 provides that physical violence against minors as a means of punishment in the context of their upbringing brings about the consequences of Article 1532 of the Civil Code. The explanatory memorandum to this article states, among other things: “The regulation of Article 4 makes it clear that corporal punishment against children is not included in the permissible punishment measures of Article 1518 of the Civil Code in accordance with modern pedagogical views. It constitutes a case of poor exercise of custody and for this reason brings about the application of article 1532 of the Civil Code. According to this article, in such a case, the court may order any appropriate measure. "Any act of inflicting pain or physical discomfort on a minor should be treated as physical violence, with the aim of punishing or controlling his behavior."

In Ireland, all forms of corporal punishment of children have been definitively outlawed since the passing of the Children First Act 2015.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46)Law in the Republic of Ireland inherited the pre-independence common law and statutes modelled on English law. These included allowance under common law of "physical chastisement" by teachers, and under the Children Act 1908 (8 Edw. 7. c. 67) of "reasonable chastisement" by parents and those _in loco parentis_.

School corporal punishment was prohibited in 1982 by an administrative decision of John Boland, the Minister for Education.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-dail20151021-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-48) Teachers were not liable to criminal prosecution until 1997, when the rule of law allowing physical chastisement was explicitly abolished.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-49) The Children Act 2001 repealed the 1908 act but, except in children detention schools, did not explicitly prohibit corporal punishment;[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-it1512623-51) the common-law defence of "reasonable chastisement" remained available to parents facing a charge of assault.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-it1512623-51)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46) In response to a complaint filed with the European Committee of Social Rights,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-52) the defence was abolished under the Children First Act 2015.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-53)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-dail20151021-47)

School corporal punishment became prohibited in 1928. In 1996, the Supreme Court of Italy ruled that in domestic settings, physical punishment is no longer an acceptable way to discipline children.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-54) However, that is still yet to be confirmed in legislation.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-55)
In India, corporal punishment is banned in schools, daycare and alternative child care institutions. However, there are no prohibitions of it at home. The National Policy for Children 2013 states that in education, the state shall “ensure no child is subjected to any physical punishment or mental harassment” and “promote positive engagement to impart discipline so as to provide children with a good learning experience”. Corporal punishment is prohibited in schools in the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 (RTE Act). Article 17 states: “(1) No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment. (2) Whoever contravenes the provisions of sub-section (1) shall be liable to disciplinary action under the service rules applicable to such person.” Guidance (”Advisory for Eliminating Corporal Punishment in Schools under Section 35(1) of the RTE Act 2009”) which sets out the national law relevant to corporal punishment in schools, the international human rights standards, steps that may be taken to promote positive child development and not resorting to corporal punishment, and the role of national bodies in implementing the RTE Act, stating: “This advisory should be used by the State Governments/UT Administrations to ensure that appropriate State/school level guidelines on prevention of corporate punishment and appropriate redressal of any complaints, are framed, disseminated, acted upon and monitored.”[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-57)

According to Vasudev Sharma, the executive director of Child Rights Trust, Bengaluru, "Many teachers hauled up for corporal punishment claim protection under Sections 88 and 89 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) saying they were taking action in good faith." Section 88 protects "Acts not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person’s benefit" and Section 89 "act[s] done in good faith for benefit of child or insane person, by or by consent of guardian."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-58)
On 25 January 2000, the Supreme Court of Israel issued the landmark _Plonit_ decision ruling that "corporal punishment of children by their parents is never educational", "always causes serious harm to the children" and "is indefensible".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel1-59) This decision repealed section 7 of article 27 of the Civil Wrongs Ordinance 1944, which provided a defence for the use of corporal punishment in childrearing, and stated that "the law imposes an obligation on state authorities to intervene in the family unit and to protect the child when necessary, including from his parents."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel2-60) As a result, all kinds of physical discipline against children were automatically banned through the country, as confirmed by multiple subsequent court rulings.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel3-61)
In September 2018, Nepal adopted the "Children's act 2018" which criminalises corporal punishment of children in all settings.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-The_Himalayan_Times_2018-62)

The Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007 or "anti-smacking bill" was introduced as a member's bill by Green Party Member of Parliament Sue Bradford in 2005 passed on its third reading on 16 May 2007 by 113 votes to eight.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-64)
The 2009 New Zealand citizens-initiated referendum posed the question: "Should a smack as part of good parental correction be a criminal offence in New Zealand?"[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-65) 87.4% of votes answered "No". The referendum was non-binding and did not lead to a change in the law. It was noted at the time that "the wording of the proposition was misleading and ambiguous".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-66)
School corporal punishment was explicitly prohibited in 1936. In 1972, an 1891 law that gave parents some right to use corporal punishment of their children was removed from the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, which made corporal punishment of children unlawful and punishable as assault. In order to clarify that violence towards children is not allowed, an explicit ban on corporal punishment of children came into force in 1987.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-67)

# Global Progress Toward Prohibiting Corporal Punishment


# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
While Canada’s progress on abolishing Section 43 and upholding children’s rights has remained stagnant, other States Parties to the Convention have advanced to implementing children’s rights to full protection under the law. Table 1 presents the 65 States, 2 nations and 16 territories that have prohibited corporal punishment of children in all settings over the past 44 years (End Corporal Punishment, 2023). An additional 27 States have committed to full prohibition, meaning that they have introduced or are actively supporting legislative initiatives, have expressed clear support for recommendations to prohibit corporal punishment during periodic reviews, have publicly expressed support for awareness-raising and law reform advocacy initiatives, and/or have committed to full prohibition via official communication to End Corporal Punishment (End Corporal Punishment, 2023). Most recently, in May 2023, I ndia, Indonesia, Morocco and the Philippines accepted recommendations to prohibit corporal punishment.  To date, Canada has not made any such formal commitment. 18

The significance of law reform lies in its ability to provide clear guidance to parents, teachers, alternative caregivers, social services and law enforcement and society as a whole on what acts are socially acceptable and which acts are not - in this case, to signal that it is no longer acceptable or lawful to hit a child any more than it is to hit anyone else, and to affirm children’s rights to physical protection. Law reform alone is not sufficient to eliminate corporal punishment of children, but it does raise awareness of its harms and influences social norms and behaviour change (e.g., parenting practices and child welfare guidance) by redefining dominant attitudes and beliefs ( End Corporal Punishment, 2021).
The primary aims of law reform are preventative and educational and to ensure that children have equal legal protection without exceptions. In the majority of countries that have reformed their laws, this has been done by 1) abolishing the common law defence; and/or 2) removing the criminal and/or civil defence of “reasonable chastisement” or “corrective force.” Many countries have gone beyond removing defences to introduce an explicit prohibition on corporal punishment in their statutes. Although such legislative reforms technically “criminalize” corporal punishment as assault, there is no evidence of increased prosecution of parents in countries that have implemented such reforms (End Corporal Punishment, 2019). These laws are implemented with careful consideration of children’s best interests and in alignment with countries’ existing laws on assault.

# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Two principles guide the implementation of corporal punishment law. The first is the UN CRC’s Article 3, the Best Interests of the Child principle. This standard ensures that the enactment of corporal punishment laws is done with consideration of the child’s best interests, including the importance of family relationships and children’s dependence on their caregivers. Based on this principle, the decision to prosecute parents or intervene in family life should be 20
made cautiously and with great care and only when the risk for significant harm is evidenced (End Corporal Punishment, 2019). The second consideration is the  de minimis principle. This legal principle is derived from the Latin phrase ‘ de minimis non curat lex’ , which translates to “the law cares not for small things’ or, in other words, the law does not concern itself with trivial matters (End Corporal Punishment, 2019).  This principle ensures that minor assaults are only prosecuted in exceptional circumstances. Should a case of corporal punishment come to the attention of authorities,  a first response would be to focus on supportive and educational efforts that provide caregivers with alternatives to corporal punishment that uphold children’s rights to equal protection under the law. Again, the purpose of these laws is to educate, not to punish parents.
Laws are powerful symbols of societal values. They set standards for what is acceptable in a society. In Canada, Section 43 communicates that corporal punishment of children is not only acceptable but justifiable - that is, the right thing to do. When countries enact laws stating that corporal punishment of children is neither justifiable nor acceptable, they expect that societal values will shift, reflected in attitudes and behaviour – particularly when accompanied by public education and parent support. Has this been the case?  Sweden, Germany, and New Zealand have both enacted full corporal punishment prohibitions and collected longitudinal and population-level data. In this section, I summarize findings from those three countries.
Outcomes of Law Reform in Sweden

# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Sweden was the first country in the world to legally prohibit physical punishment against children in all settings (see Durrant, 1999; Durrant & Janson, 2005; Durrant & Olsen, 1997; Durrant, 2019). This process began in 1929 when Sweden prohibited corporal punishment in secondary schools. Half a century later, in 1957, as lawmakers recognized the extent of violence against children taking place in homes, they removed the criminal defence to corrective assault of a child from the Penal Code . Realizing that the civil Parental Code (Föräldrabalken ) still contained a paragraph permitting “mild” physical punishment, lawmakers removed that paragraph in 1966 to ensure consistency across laws. However, the death of a child in 1971 due to physical maltreatment, followed by a 1975 legal judgment acquitting a father who had severely beaten his child, led the Minister of Justice to appoint a Commission on Children’s Rights with a mandate to review the Parental Code . The Commission proposed the addition of a 21
paragraph to the Parental Code making explicit that no physical punishment of children was permitted. The proposal was supported by all political parties and 98% of members of the Swedish Parliament. It came into force on July 1, 1979. The paragraph states:
Children are entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. Children are to be treated with respect for their person and individuality and may not be subjected to physical punishment or other injurious or humiliating treatment (Department of Justice, 2023; ch. 6.1).

# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Rather than setting out what adults are allowed to do to children, this law clearly states that children have the right to respect and full protection. There is no “grey area” or “zone of non-abusive assault” (McGillivray & Durrant, 2022, p. 412). As the ban came into force, the Department of Justice implemented the largest public education campaign in Sweden’s history (Durrant & Olsen, 1997; Ziegert, 1983). A 16-page leaflet was translated into all immigrant languages and distributed to all households with young children that explained the law’s rationale and provided information about ways to raise children without corporal punishment. Information was printed on milk cartons for two months to promote discussion of the issue among families at mealtime, and to make the law highly visible. The aim of the campaign was to raise public awareness of the law and to educate caregivers on raising children without violence (see Modig, 2014; Waterston & Janson, 2020).

# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Evidence of the positive impact of the ban in Sweden is robust and consistent (Durrant, 1999, 2000, 2003; Durrant, & Janson, 2005; Janson et al., 2011; Lansford et al., 2010; Modig, 2014). In the 1950s, corporal punishment of children was common in Sweden, and beliefs about the necessity of corporal punishment in child-rearing were widespread. For example, in 1965, 14 years prior to the ban, about half the adult population believed that corporal punishment was necessary for raising children. By 1971, that proportion had declined to 35%; by 1981, two years following the ban, it had declined to 29% (Durrant, 2003). By 2009, 30 years following the introduction of the ban, the proportion of adults who believed in the necessity of corporal punishment had reached nearly zero (see Figure 1; Lansford et al., 2010; Modig, 2014). In a study comparing parental attitudes in China, Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, Philippines, Sweden, Thailand and the US, it was only in Sweden where no parent believed that corporal punishment was necessary in bringing up children (Lansford et al., 2010). In 2011, 32 years following the ban's introduction, 92% of Swedish parents surveyed indicated that it was “wrong 22
to hit or slap a child, even if the child had made the parent very angry” (Janson, Jernbro & Långberg, 2011, p. 5).
Figure 1. The Percentage of Swedish Adults Who Believe That Corporal Punishment Is Necessary (Swedish Institute for Opinion Surveys, 1981; Lansford et al., 2010).

# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
An assessment of trends in Swedish parents’ use of corporal punishment reveals a similar decline. In the 1980s, shortly following the introduction of the ban, 28% of Swedish parents surveyed reported hitting their children in the previous year. By the 2000s, that proportion had been reduced to virtually zero (Durrant, 2019; Janson, Jernbro & Långberg, 2011; Statistics Sweden, 1996). In 2011, 86% of 15- and 16-year-olds reported that they had never experienced physical punishment; of those who had, only 3% had experienced it several times (Janson, Jernbro & Långberg, 2011).
Outcomes of Law Reform in Germany
In 2000, Germany passed the Act to Prohibit Violence in the Upbringing of the Child .This Act placed an explicit prohibition into the German Civil Code 2002, which states: “Children have the right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological injuries and other humiliating measures are prohibited” (Federal Ministry of Justice, 2002, Article 1631(2)). Preceding and accompanying the law was extensive public discussion to raise awareness and begin to reframe previously normalized behaviour as harmful and socially unacceptable.

# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
A comparison of German parents’ beliefs eight years before the ban and one year after revealed a notable shift. In 1992, 31% of parents surveyed believed that slaps “make children see reason.” By 2001, that proportion had dropped to 26%. Before the ban, 49% agreed that “smacking teaches children to accept violence.” That proportion increased to nearly 60% by 2001 (Bussmann, 2004). In 1992, youth were far more likely than youth in 2002 to report having experienced various forms of corporal punishment, including being slapped across the face (81% vs. 69%), being hit on the bottom (41% vs. 5%), and being bruised (31% vs. 3%) (see Figure 2). By 2007, 28% of German parents surveyed had never used corporal punishment, and nearly 90% believed that non-violent child-rearing is ideal (see Bussmann, 2010). A comparative study of 9,500 youth and adults’ experiences of violence during childhood found that the proportion of individuals in Germany who had experienced ‘light’ violence in childhood had decreased from 58% in 1992 to 36% in 2011. This same study found that 16-20-year-olds were more likely to have never been physically punished (63%) compared to older adults (Pfeiffer, 2012).
Figure 2. The Percentage of Youth In Germany Who Reported Ever Experiencing Various Forms Of Corporal Punishment in 1992 and 2002 (Bussman, 2004).
Outcomes of Law Reform in New Zealand
Until 2007, New Zealand’s Crimes Act 1961 provided a defence to reasonable force by way of correction. The wording of this law was identical to Canada’s Section 43, except that teachers had been removed from the defence in 1989 (Durrant, 2019). The defence was repealed in 2007 when the Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007 was passed

The significance of law reform lies in its ability to provide clear guidance to parents, teachers, alternative caregivers, social services and law enforcement and society as a whole on what acts are socially acceptable and which acts are not - in this case, to signal that it is no longer acceptable or lawful to hit a child any more than it is to hit anyone else, and to affirm children’s rights to physical protection. Law reform alone is not sufficient to eliminate corporal punishment of children, but it does raise awareness of its harms and influences social norms and behaviour change (e.g., parenting practices and child welfare guidance) by redefining dominant attitudes and beliefs ( End Corporal Punishment, 2021).
The primary aims of law reform are preventative and educational and to ensure that children have equal legal protection without exceptions. In the majority of countries that have reformed their laws, this has been done by 1) abolishing the common law defence; and/or 2) removing the criminal and/or civil defence of “reasonable chastisement” or “corrective force.” Many countries have gone beyond removing defences to introduce an explicit prohibition on corporal punishment in their statutes. Although such legislative reforms technically “criminalize” corporal punishment as assault, there is no evidence of increased prosecution of parents in countries that have implemented such reforms (End Corporal Punishment, 2019). These laws are implemented with careful consideration of children’s best interests and in alignment with countries’ existing laws on assault.
texts.19:
# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Two principles guide the implementation of corporal punishment law. The first is the UN CRC’s Article 3, the Best Interests of the Child principle. This standard ensures that the enactment of corporal punishment laws is done with consideration of the child’s best interests, including the importance of family relationships and children’s dependence on their caregivers. Based on this principle, the decision to prosecute parents or intervene in family life should be 20
made cautiously and with great care and only when the risk for significant harm is evidenced (End Corporal Punishment, 2019). The second consideration is the  de minimis principle. This legal principle is derived from the Latin phrase ‘ de minimis non curat lex’ , which translates to “the law cares not for small things’ or, in other words, the law does not concern itself with trivial matters (End Corporal Punishment, 2019).  This principle ensures that minor assaults are only prosecuted in exceptional circumstances. Should a case of corporal punishment come to the attention of authorities,  a first response would be to focus on supportive and educational efforts that provide caregivers with alternatives to corporal punishment that uphold children’s rights to equal protection under the law. Again, the purpose of these laws is to educate, not to punish parents.
Laws are powerful symbols of societal values. They set standards for what is acceptable in a society. In Canada, Section 43 communicates that corporal punishment of children is not only acceptable but justifiable - that is, the right thing to do. When countries enact laws stating that corporal punishment of children is neither justifiable nor acceptable, they expect that societal values will shift, reflected in attitudes and behaviour – particularly when accompanied by public education and parent support. Has this been the case?  Sweden, Germany, and New Zealand have both enacted full corporal punishment prohibitions and collected longitudinal and population-level data. In this section, I summarize findings from those three countries.
Outcomes of Law Reform in Sweden
texts.20:
# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Sweden was the first country in the world to legally prohibit physical punishment against children in all settings (see Durrant, 1999; Durrant & Janson, 2005; Durrant & Olsen, 1997; Durrant, 2019). This process began in 1929 when Sweden prohibited corporal punishment in secondary schools. Half a century later, in 1957, as lawmakers recognized the extent of violence against children taking place in homes, they removed the criminal defence to corrective assault of a child from the Penal Code . Realizing that the civil Parental Code (Föräldrabalken ) still contained a paragraph permitting “mild” physical punishment, lawmakers removed that paragraph in 1966 to ensure consistency across laws. However, the death of a child in 1971 due to physical maltreatment, followed by a 1975 legal judgment acquitting a father who had severely beaten his child, led the Minister of Justice to appoint a Commission on Children’s Rights with a mandate to review the Parental Code . The Commission proposed the addition of a 21
paragraph to the Parental Code making explicit that no physical punishment of children was permitted. The proposal was supported by all political parties and 98% of members of the Swedish Parliament. It came into force on July 1, 1979. The paragraph states:
Children are entitled to care, security and a good upbringing. Children are to be treated with respect for their person and individuality and may not be subjected to physical punishment or other injurious or humiliating treatment (Department of Justice, 2023; ch. 6.1).
texts.21:
# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Rather than setting out what adults are allowed to do to children, this law clearly states that children have the right to respect and full protection. There is no “grey area” or “zone of non-abusive assault” (McGillivray & Durrant, 2022, p. 412). As the ban came into force, the Department of Justice implemented the largest public education campaign in Sweden’s history (Durrant & Olsen, 1997; Ziegert, 1983). A 16-page leaflet was translated into all immigrant languages and distributed to all households with young children that explained the law’s rationale and provided information about ways to raise children without corporal punishment. Information was printed on milk cartons for two months to promote discussion of the issue among families at mealtime, and to make the law highly visible. The aim of the campaign was to raise public awareness of the law and to educate caregivers on raising children without violence (see Modig, 2014; Waterston & Janson, 2020).
texts.22:
# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
Evidence of the positive impact of the ban in Sweden is robust and consistent (Durrant, 1999, 2000, 2003; Durrant, & Janson, 2005; Janson et al., 2011; Lansford et al., 2010; Modig, 2014). In the 1950s, corporal punishment of children was common in Sweden, and beliefs about the necessity of corporal punishment in child-rearing were widespread. For example, in 1965, 14 years prior to the ban, about half the adult population believed that corporal punishment was necessary for raising children. By 1971, that proportion had declined to 35%; by 1981, two years following the ban, it had declined to 29% (Durrant, 2003). By 2009, 30 years following the introduction of the ban, the proportion of adults who believed in the necessity of corporal punishment had reached nearly zero (see Figure 1; Lansford et al., 2010; Modig, 2014). In a study comparing parental attitudes in China, Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, Philippines, Sweden, Thailand and the US, it was only in Sweden where no parent believed that corporal punishment was necessary in bringing up children (Lansford et al., 2010). In 2011, 32 years following the ban's introduction, 92% of Swedish parents surveyed indicated that it was “wrong 22
to hit or slap a child, even if the child had made the parent very angry” (Janson, Jernbro & Långberg, 2011, p. 5).
Figure 1. The Percentage of Swedish Adults Who Believe That Corporal Punishment Is Necessary (Swedish Institute for Opinion Surveys, 1981; Lansford et al., 2010).
texts.23:
# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
An assessment of trends in Swedish parents’ use of corporal punishment reveals a similar decline. In the 1980s, shortly following the introduction of the ban, 28% of Swedish parents surveyed reported hitting their children in the previous year. By the 2000s, that proportion had been reduced to virtually zero (Durrant, 2019; Janson, Jernbro & Långberg, 2011; Statistics Sweden, 1996). In 2011, 86% of 15- and 16-year-olds reported that they had never experienced physical punishment; of those who had, only 3% had experienced it several times (Janson, Jernbro & Långberg, 2011).
Outcomes of Law Reform in Germany
In 2000, Germany passed the Act to Prohibit Violence in the Upbringing of the Child .This Act placed an explicit prohibition into the German Civil Code 2002, which states: “Children have the right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological injuries and other humiliating measures are prohibited” (Federal Ministry of Justice, 2002, Article 1631(2)). Preceding and accompanying the law was extensive public discussion to raise awareness and begin to reframe previously normalized behaviour as harmful and socially unacceptable.

texts.24:
# Countries, Nations, and Territories with Equal Protection for Children
A comparison of German parents’ beliefs eight years before the ban and one year after revealed a notable shift. In 1992, 31% of parents surveyed believed that slaps “make children see reason.” By 2001, that proportion had dropped to 26%. Before the ban, 49% agreed that “smacking teaches children to accept violence.” That proportion increased to nearly 60% by 2001 (Bussmann, 2004). In 1992, youth were far more likely than youth in 2002 to report having experienced various forms of corporal punishment, including being slapped across the face (81% vs. 69%), being hit on the bottom (41% vs. 5%), and being bruised (31% vs. 3%) (see Figure 2). By 2007, 28% of German parents surveyed had never used corporal punishment, and nearly 90% believed that non-violent child-rearing is ideal (see Bussmann, 2010). A comparative study of 9,500 youth and adults’ experiences of violence during childhood found that the proportion of individuals in Germany who had experienced ‘light’ violence in childhood had decreased from 58% in 1992 to 36% in 2011. This same study found that 16-20-year-olds were more likely to have never been physically punished (63%) compared to older adults (Pfeiffer, 2012).
Figure 2. The Percentage of Youth In Germany Who Reported Ever Experiencing Various Forms Of Corporal Punishment in 1992 and 2002 (Bussman, 2004).
Outcomes of Law Reform in New Zealand
Until 2007, New Zealand’s Crimes Act 1961 provided a defence to reasonable force by way of correction. The wording of this law was identical to Canada’s Section 43, except that teachers had been removed from the defence in 1989 (Durrant, 2019). The defence was repealed in 2007 when the Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007 was passed

texts.4:
In upholding section 43, the majority of the Court provided considerable guidance to the interpretation of the provision. The majority held that the person administering the discipline must be a parent or legal guardian, or in some cases, a school teacher (i.e. non-parental relatives such as grandparents, aunts, or uncles, as well as babysitters and other caretakers, are banned from spanking); that the force must be used "by way of correction" (sober, reasoned uses of force that address the actual behaviour of the child and are designed to restrain, control or express some symbolic disapproval of his or her behaviour), that the child must be capable of benefiting from the correction (i.e. not under the age of 2 or over 12), and that the use of force must be "reasonable under the circumstances", meaning that it results neither in harm nor in the prospect of bodily harm. Punishment involving slaps or blows to the head is harmful, the Court held.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-33) Use of any implement other than a bare hand is illegal and hitting a child in anger or in retaliation for something a child did is not considered reasonable and is against the law. The Court defined "reasonable" as force that would have a "transitory and trifling" impact on the child. For example, spanking or slapping a child so hard that it leaves a mark that lasts for several hours would not be considered "transitory and trifling".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-34)
Among the recommendations of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, formed to redress the legacy of the Canadian Indian residential school system, is a call to repeal Section 43 of the Criminal Code.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-35)
On 23 March 2021, the Senate of Colombia unanimously voted to approve a bill that prohibits physical punishment, cruel, humiliating, or degrading acts, and violence as forms of correctional approaches for the upbringing of children and adolescents in Colombia.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-36)
texts.5:
Until 2026, the Czech Republic had remained the only country in the European Union that does not outlaw child corporal punishment or plan to introduce such a law.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-37) On July 17, 2025, the president signed an amendment to the Civil Code, making corporal punishment of children explicitly prohibited by law, beginning January 1, 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-cz-16)
Corporal punishment in schools in Denmark became explicitly prohibited in 1967 and in 1985, parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children became outlawed through a new law which required parents "to protect their child from physical and psychological violence and other humiliating treatment".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-39) However, the law was believed to still support corporal punishment as there was a controversy whether the law permitted parents to punish their children physically or otherwise.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-40) Therefore, after several years of debate, a new, clearer law came into force on 28 May 1997, providing that "_The child has right to care and security. It must be treated with respect for its person and must not be subjected to corporal punishment or other humiliating treatment_".
Denmark's autonomous territories, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, banned corporal punishment of children in 2007 and 2016, respectively.
texts.6:
School corporal punishment was banned in 1914.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-41) Parents' right to use corporal punishment of their children was outlawed in 1969 when the section in the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, stating that a "petty assault" was not punishable if committed by parents or others who exercise their right to chastise a child, was removed. In 1983, corporal punishment of children was explicitly banned.
In the Napoleonic era parents were explicitly allowed to physically punish their children. Spanking was previously popular, with 85% of French parents admitting to using it. However, in 2019, the National Assembly approved a bill introducing a complete ban on all forms of physical punishment of children and required mayors officiating at civil weddings to remind couples that violence against children is unlawful.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-auto-7) The law makes corporal punishment a civil offense, not a criminal one.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-42)
School corporal punishment was prohibited in East Germany (which became part of the Federal Republic of Germany at the German reunification on 3 October 1990). In the Federal Republic (West Germany before reunification), it was prohibited at different times in its different states between 1975 and 1983.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-43)
texts.7:
In the Federal Republic of Germany, in 1980 it became prohibited for parents to educate their children with "degrading measures" (it was not clear exactly what "degrading" meant), of which the common interpretation was that corporal punishment of children was still permitted as long as it was not "degrading". On 1 July 1998, corporal punishment was outlawed through a new law stating that "Degrading educational measures, especially physical and psychological maltreatment, are inadmissible"; the common interpretation of that law was that parents still had some right to use corporal punishment on their children. In November 2000, that law was replaced with a new more clear and strict law stating that "_Children have right to a non-violent upbringing. Corporal punishment, psychological violence and other degrading educational measures are inadmissible._"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-45)
The 2006 enacted Law 3500/06 on the treatment of domestic violence prohibits the use of physical violence against a minor as a means of punishment in the context of his upbringing, with the explicit clarification - in the explanatory memorandum - that corporal punishment is not included. to the permissible penitentiary measures of article 1518 of the Civil Code and that its use entails for the parents the consequences of the bad exercise of parental care.
Specifically, Article 4 provides that physical violence against minors as a means of punishment in the context of their upbringing brings about the consequences of Article 1532 of the Civil Code. The explanatory memorandum to this article states, among other things: “The regulation of Article 4 makes it clear that corporal punishment against children is not included in the permissible punishment measures of Article 1518 of the Civil Code in accordance with modern pedagogical views. It constitutes a case of poor exercise of custody and for this reason brings about the application of article 1532 of the Civil Code. According to this article, in such a case, the court may order any appropriate measure. "Any act of inflicting pain or physical discomfort on a minor should be treated as physical violence, with the aim of punishing or controlling his behavior."
texts.8: In Ireland, all forms of corporal punishment of children have been definitively outlawed since the passing of the Children First Act 2015.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46)Law in the Republic of Ireland inherited the pre-independence common law and statutes modelled on English law. These included allowance under common law of "physical chastisement" by teachers, and under the Children Act 1908 (8 Edw. 7. c. 67) of "reasonable chastisement" by parents and those _in loco parentis_.
texts.9: School corporal punishment was prohibited in 1982 by an administrative decision of John Boland, the Minister for Education.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-dail20151021-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-48) Teachers were not liable to criminal prosecution until 1997, when the rule of law allowing physical chastisement was explicitly abolished.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-49) The Children Act 2001 repealed the 1908 act but, except in children detention schools, did not explicitly prohibit corporal punishment;[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-it1512623-51) the common-law defence of "reasonable chastisement" remained available to parents facing a charge of assault.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-it1512623-51)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-endcorporalpunishment_ireland-46) In response to a complaint filed with the European Committee of Social Rights,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-52) the defence was abolished under the Children First Act 2015.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-53)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-dail20151021-47)
texts.10:
School corporal punishment became prohibited in 1928. In 1996, the Supreme Court of Italy ruled that in domestic settings, physical punishment is no longer an acceptable way to discipline children.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-54) However, that is still yet to be confirmed in legislation.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-55)
In India, corporal punishment is banned in schools, daycare and alternative child care institutions. However, there are no prohibitions of it at home. The National Policy for Children 2013 states that in education, the state shall “ensure no child is subjected to any physical punishment or mental harassment” and “promote positive engagement to impart discipline so as to provide children with a good learning experience”. Corporal punishment is prohibited in schools in the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 (RTE Act). Article 17 states: “(1) No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment. (2) Whoever contravenes the provisions of sub-section (1) shall be liable to disciplinary action under the service rules applicable to such person.” Guidance (”Advisory for Eliminating Corporal Punishment in Schools under Section 35(1) of the RTE Act 2009”) which sets out the national law relevant to corporal punishment in schools, the international human rights standards, steps that may be taken to promote positive child development and not resorting to corporal punishment, and the role of national bodies in implementing the RTE Act, stating: “This advisory should be used by the State Governments/UT Administrations to ensure that appropriate State/school level guidelines on prevention of corporate punishment and appropriate redressal of any complaints, are framed, disseminated, acted upon and monitored.”[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-57)
texts.11:
According to Vasudev Sharma, the executive director of Child Rights Trust, Bengaluru, "Many teachers hauled up for corporal punishment claim protection under Sections 88 and 89 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) saying they were taking action in good faith." Section 88 protects "Acts not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person’s benefit" and Section 89 "act[s] done in good faith for benefit of child or insane person, by or by consent of guardian."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-58)
On 25 January 2000, the Supreme Court of Israel issued the landmark _Plonit_ decision ruling that "corporal punishment of children by their parents is never educational", "always causes serious harm to the children" and "is indefensible".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel1-59) This decision repealed section 7 of article 27 of the Civil Wrongs Ordinance 1944, which provided a defence for the use of corporal punishment in childrearing, and stated that "the law imposes an obligation on state authorities to intervene in the family unit and to protect the child when necessary, including from his parents."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel2-60) As a result, all kinds of physical discipline against children were automatically banned through the country, as confirmed by multiple subsequent court rulings.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-israel3-61)
In September 2018, Nepal adopted the "Children's act 2018" which criminalises corporal punishment of children in all settings.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-The_Himalayan_Times_2018-62)
texts.12:
The Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007 or "anti-smacking bill" was introduced as a member's bill by Green Party Member of Parliament Sue Bradford in 2005 passed on its third reading on 16 May 2007 by 113 votes to eight.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-64)
The 2009 New Zealand citizens-initiated referendum posed the question: "Should a smack as part of good parental correction be a criminal offence in New Zealand?"[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-65) 87.4% of votes answered "No". The referendum was non-binding and did not lead to a change in the law. It was noted at the time that "the wording of the proposition was misleading and ambiguous".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-66)
School corporal punishment was explicitly prohibited in 1936. In 1972, an 1891 law that gave parents some right to use corporal punishment of their children was removed from the constitution of assault in the Penal Code, which made corporal punishment of children unlawful and punishable as assault. In order to clarify that violence towards children is not allowed, an explicit ban on corporal punishment of children came into force in 1987.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_corporal_punishment_laws#cite_note-67)

## Delay
It is well over 30 years since the UN General Assembly adopted the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, in 1989. And yet still the law in far too many countries does not prohibit corporal punishment of children, or worse it explicitly authorises its use and sets out the details of how it should be inflicted. There is still a long way to go:
*    Only 15% of the world's children are fully protected in law from all corporal punishment   
*    Governments of 105 states are not currently committed to law reform   
*    In 62 states corporal punishment has not been fully prohibited in schools
**In 15 states, corporal punishment is not fully prohibited in any setting, including as a sentence for crime:**
Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Eritrea; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tuvalu; UR Tanzania
**In 29 states, corporal punishment – whipping, flogging, caning – is still lawful under state, traditional and/or religious law as a sentence for crimes committed by juveniles:**

### Risks for school administrators
Furthermore, while corporal punishment is sometimes lauded as an alternative to suspension, the lack of formal training for U.S. teachers means that there is no consistently implemented style of corporal punishment that takes into account the size, age, or psychological profile of students. This leaves students more vulnerable to physical and psychological injury.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-sparks2-49)
In November 2018 the American Academy of Pediatrics issued a new policy statement taking a stronger stance against corporal punishment, including spanking, twenty years after releasing its last position statement on effective discipline._[citation needed_]
The AAP mentioned in particular the risks on mental health issues and anger management problems, in children and teens who received corporal punishments in school._[citation needed_]
Public-opinion research has found that most Americans are not in favor of school corporal punishment; in polls taken in 2002 and 2005, American adults were respectively 72% and 77% opposed to the use of corporal punishment by teachers.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-75) Moreover, a national survey conducted on teachers ranked corporal punishment as the least effective method to discipline offenders among eight possible techniques.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-76)
A bill to end the use of corporal punishment in schools was introduced into the United States House of Representatives in June 2010 during the 111th Congress.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-78) The bill, H.R. 5628,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-79) was referred to the United States House Committee on Education and Labor, where it was not brought up for a vote.

### Risks for school administrators
The United States' National Association of Secondary School Principals (NASSP) opposes the use of corporal punishment in schools, defined as the deliberate infliction of pain in response to students' unacceptable behavior or language. In articulating its opposition, it cites the disproportionate use of corporal punishment on black students; potential adverse effects on students' self-image and school achievement; correlation between school corporal punishment and increased truancy, drop-out rates, violence, and vandalism by youth; the potential for misuse or injury to students; and increased liability for schools.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-80)
Some scholars, such as Elizabeth Gershoff and Sarah Font, perceive a double standard when it comes to the physical punishment of children versus adults. The Board of Education in Pickens County, Alabama recommends that teachers use a two-foot-long paddle to discipline children;[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-81) in some cases, this object is more than half the height of an elementary school-aged child.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDC-82) The two scholars assert that in any other context, "the act of an adult hitting another person with a board [two feet long] (or really, of any size) would be considered assault with a weapon and would be punishable under criminal law".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-:02-23)
However, some teachers and administrators[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-auto-83) defend the use of corporal punishment in the classroom as a reasonable alternative to other types of disciplinary action, like suspension, which have been shown to negatively impact children's classroom performance and social skills.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_corporal_punishment_in_the_United_States#cite_note-suspension-84)

*   Hazing in fraternities and sororities  
*   Corporal punishment in the home  
*   Judicial corporal punishment

## Delay
It is well over 30 years since the UN General Assembly adopted the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, in 1989. And yet still the law in far too many countries does not prohibit corporal punishment of children, or worse it explicitly authorises its use and sets out the details of how it should be inflicted. There is still a long way to go:
*    Only 15% of the world's children are fully protected in law from all corporal punishment   
*    Governments of 105 states are not currently committed to law reform   
*    In 62 states corporal punishment has not been fully prohibited in schools
**In 15 states, corporal punishment is not fully prohibited in any setting, including as a sentence for crime:**
Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Eritrea; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tuvalu; UR Tanzania
**In 29 states, corporal punishment – whipping, flogging, caning – is still lawful under state, traditional and/or religious law as a sentence for crimes committed by juveniles:**
Afghanistan; Bahamas; Bangladesh; Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Ecuador; Eritrea; India; Indonesia; Iran; Kiribati; Libya; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Qatar; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tonga; Tuvalu; United Arab Emirates; UR Tanzania; Vanuatu; Yemen

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
School corporal punishment, historically widespread, was outlawed in different states via their administrative law at different times. It was not completely abolished everywhere until 1983.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-97) Since 1993, use of corporal punishment by a teacher has been a criminal offence. In that year a sentence by the Federal Court of Justice of Germany (_Bundesgerichtshof_, case number NStZ 1993.591) was published which overruled the previous powers enshrined in unofficial customary law (_Gewohnheitsrecht_) and upheld by some regional appeal courts (_Oberlandesgericht_, Superior State Court) even in the 1970s. They assumed a _right of chastisement_ was a defense of justification against the accusation of "causing bodily harm" per _Paragraph_ (=Section) _223 Strafgesetzbuch_ (Federal Penal Code).
Corporal punishment in Greek primary schools was banned in 1998, and in secondary schools in 2005.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-98)

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
In India, corporal punishment is banned in schools, daycare and alternative child care institutions. The National Policy for Children 2013 states that in education, the state shall "ensure no child is subjected to any physical punishment or mental harassment" and "promote positive engagement to impart discipline so as to provide children with a good learning experience". Corporal punishment is also prohibited by the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 (RTE Act). Article 17 states: "(1) No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment. (2) Whoever contravenes the provisions of sub-section (1) shall be liable to disciplinary action under the service rules applicable to such person." The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Rules 2010 provide for implementation of the Act, including awareness raising about the rights in the Act, procedures for monitoring implementation, and complaints mechanisms when the rights are violated. In 2014, the Ministry of Human Resources Development issued guidance ("Advisory for Eliminating Corporal Punishment in Schools under Section 35(1) of the RTE Act 2009") which sets out the national law relevant to corporal punishment in schools, the international human rights standards, steps that may be taken to promote positive child development and not resorting to corporal punishment, and the role of national bodies in implementing the RTE Act, stating: "This advisory should be used by the State Governments/UT Administrations to ensure that appropriate State/school level guidelines on prevention of corporate punishment and appropriate redressal of any complaints, are framed, disseminated, acted upon and monitored."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-100)
However, corporal punishment is still widely prevalent in schools in Indian rural communities.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-102)

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
On 10 August 2000, Iran "Supreme Council of Education" (شورای عالی آموزش وپرورش) (under supervision of Ministry of Education (Iran)(وزارت آموزش و پرورش)) approved an executive regulations for Iranian schools that any verbal and physical punishment for students are forbidden under the article no. 77.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-103) Iran parliament Islamic Consultative Assembly (مجلس شورای اسلامی) approved "Child and Adolescent Protection Law" (قانون حمایت از کودکان و نوجوانان) on 16 December 2002 citing that any harassment for children and teenager (under 18 years old) that is causing any physical/mental/moral damages is forbidden under article no.2.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-105)
In the law of the Republic of Ireland, corporal punishment was prohibited in 1982 by an administrative decision of John Boland, the Minister for Education, which applied to national schools (most primary schools) and to secondary schools receiving public funding (practically all of them).[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-106) In 1997, the rule of law allowing "physical chastisement" was explicitly abolished, and use of corporal punishment by schoolteachers became a criminal offence.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-107)
A 1994 Supreme Court ruling in _The State of Israel v Alagani_ declared that "corporal punishment cannot constitute a legitimate tool in the hands of teachers or other educators", applicable to both state and private schools.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-israel3-108)

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
On 25 January 2000, the Supreme Court of Israel issued the landmark _Plonit_ decision ruling that "corporal punishment of children by their parents is never educational", "always causes serious harm to the children" and "is indefensible".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-israel1-109) This decision repealed section 7 of article 27 of the Civil Wrongs Ordinance 1944, which provided a defence for the use of corporal punishment in childrearing, and stated that "the law imposes an obligation on state authorities to intervene in the family unit and to protect the child when necessary, including from his or her parents."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-israel2-110) Soon after, a new law (Pupils' Rights Law, 5760-2000) established (art. 10) that "it is the right of every pupil that discipline be maintained in the educational institution in conformity with human dignity and, in that regard, she or he has the right not to be subjected to corporal or degrading disciplinary measures."[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-israel3-108)
Corporal punishment in Italian schools has a long history but was officially banned in 1928.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-111) Despite the official ban, instances of corporal punishment have occasionally been reported in Italian schools, albeit infrequently and usually in rural or underfunded areas. Such cases are typically met with strong public condemnation and legal repercussions for the perpetrators.

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
Corporal punishment of children remains legal in schools, homes, alternative care and day-care centres.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-151)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-152) Harsh caning of girls and boys remains very common in schools.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-153)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-154)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-155)
Corporal punishment is legal in Singapore schools, for male students only (it is illegal to inflict it on female students) and fully encouraged by the government in order to maintain discipline.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-156) Only a light rattan cane may be used.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-157) This is administered in a formal ceremony by the school management after due deliberation, not by classroom teachers. Most secondary schools (whether independent, autonomous, or government-controlled), and also some primary schools, use caning to deal with misconduct by boys.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-158) At the secondary level, the rattan strokes are nearly always delivered to the student's clothed buttocks. The Ministry of Education has stipulated a maximum of three strokes per occasion. In some cases, the punishment is carried out in front of the rest of the school instead of in private.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-159)
The use of corporal punishment in schools was prohibited by the South African Schools Act, 1996. According to section 10 of the act:

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
> (1) No person may administer corporal punishment at a school to a learner.  
>   
>   
> (2) Any person who contravenes subsection (1) is guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a sentence which could be imposed for assault.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-160)
In the case of _Christian Education South Africa v Minister of Education_ the Constitutional Court rejected a claim that the constitutional right to religious freedom entitles private Christian schools to impose corporal punishment.
Liberal regions in South Korea have completely banned all forms of caning beginning with Gyeonggi Province in 2010, followed by Seoul, Gangwon Province, Gwangju and North Jeolla Province in 2011.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-161) Other more conservative regions are governed by a national law enacted in 2011 which states that while caning is generally forbidden, it can be used indirectly to maintain school discipline.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-162)
However, caning was still known to be practised indiscriminately on both boys and girls as of 2015.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-164)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-165) Mass punishments in front of the class are common, and the large number of corporal punishment scenes in films suggest that caning is an accepted cultural norm in education.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-auto-166)

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
All corporal punishment of children in South Korea has been prohibited since March 2021.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-167)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-168)
Spain banned school corporal punishment in 1985 under article 6 of the Right to Education (Organization) Act 8/1985.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-ecp_spain-169) Those who broke this law risked losing job and career; as a result, this historically well-entrenched practice soon disappeared. Eventually, all forms of corporal punishment were banned in Spain in 2007.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-ecp_spain-169)
Corporal punishment at school has been prohibited in _folkskolestadgan_ (the elementary school ordinance) since 1 January 1958. Its use by ordinary teachers in grammar schools had been outlawed in 1928.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-170) All forms of corporal punishment of children have been outlawed in Sweden since 1966, and have been strongly enforced since 1979.
In 2006, Taiwan made corporal punishment in the school system illegal.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-171)

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
In Tanzania, corporal punishment in schools is widely practised and has led to lasting damage, including the death of a punished pupil. The Education Act of 2002 authorizes the minister in charge of education to issue regulations concerning corporal punishment. The Education (Corporal Punishment) Regulation G.N. 294 of 2002 gives the authority to order corporal punishment to the headmaster of a school, who can delegate to any teacher on a case-by-case basis. The number of strikes must not be more than four for each occurrence. The school should have a register where date, reason, name of pupil and of administering teacher, together with the number of strikes, is to be recorded.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-172)
Corporal punishment in Thai schools is officially illegal under the Ministry of Education Regulation on Student Punishment 2005.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-173)
The proverb รักวัวให้ผูกรักลูกให้ตี ( "If you love your cow, tie her up; if you love your child, beat him or her") is still considered "wisdom" and is held by many Thai parents and teachers.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-174) Corporal punishment (especially caning) on students of both genders remains common[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-175)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-176)[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-177)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-178) and accepted in practice.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-179)

## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
School corporal punishment, historically widespread, was outlawed in different states via their administrative law at different times. It was not completely abolished everywhere until 1983.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-97) Since 1993, use of corporal punishment by a teacher has been a criminal offence. In that year a sentence by the Federal Court of Justice of Germany (_Bundesgerichtshof_, case number NStZ 1993.591) was published which overruled the previous powers enshrined in unofficial customary law (_Gewohnheitsrecht_) and upheld by some regional appeal courts (_Oberlandesgericht_, Superior State Court) even in the 1970s. They assumed a _right of chastisement_ was a defense of justification against the accusation of "causing bodily harm" per _Paragraph_ (=Section) _223 Strafgesetzbuch_ (Federal Penal Code).
Corporal punishment in Greek primary schools was banned in 1998, and in secondary schools in 2005.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-98)
texts.22:
## Effects on students
### Abkhazia and South Ossetia
In India, corporal punishment is banned in schools, daycare and alternative child care institutions. The National Policy for Children 2013 states that in education, the state shall "ensure no child is subjected to any physical punishment or mental harassment" and "promote positive engagement to impart discipline so as to provide children with a good learning experience". Corporal punishment is also prohibited by the Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009 (RTE Act). Article 17 states: "(1) No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment. (2) Whoever contravenes the provisions of sub-section (1) shall be liable to disciplinary action under the service rules applicable to such person." The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Rules 2010 provide for implementation of the Act, including awareness raising about the rights in the Act, procedures for monitoring implementation, and complaints mechanisms when the rights are violated. In 2014, the Ministry of Human Resources Development issued guidance ("Advisory for Eliminating Corporal Punishment in Schools under Section 35(1) of the RTE Act 2009") which sets out the national law relevant to corporal punishment in schools, the international human rights standards, steps that may be taken to promote positive child development and not resorting to corporal punishment, and the role of national bodies in implementing the RTE Act, stating: "This advisory should be used by the State Governments/UT Administrations to ensure that appropriate State/school level guidelines on prevention of corporate punishment and appropriate redressal of any complaints, are framed, disseminated, acted upon and monitored."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-100)
However, corporal punishment is still widely prevalent in schools in Indian rural communities.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporal_punishment_in_schools#cite_note-102)
